notes.h: Background and causes of the purges
notes.b: The show trials of 1936 to 1938 were the public face of a wider Terror in which Stalin removed rivals, scapegoated officials and eliminated anyone he saw as a threat.
points: By the mid-1930s Stalin had defeated the Left and Right Oppositions, but many old Bolsheviks who had opposed him remained active in the party and the state.
The economic failures of the Five-Year Plans, including shortages and the cost of collectivisation, gave Stalin reason to find scapegoats among managers, engineers and officials.
Stalin's fear of conspiracy and his personal suspicion of rivals led him to see opposition within the party as a threat to the regime.
The Party Congress of 1934, known as the Congress of Victors, was followed by the arrest and execution of many of its delegates in the Terror.
Purges of the party began in 1933 with the expulsion of members judged unreliable, and were extended to the army and the security services in the late 1930s.
The Terror was organised by the NKVD, the secret police, under Genrikh Yagoda until 1936 and then under Nikolai Yezhov, who became People's Commissar for Internal Affairs in September 1936.

notes.h: The Kirov murder and the first trial, 1934-1936
notes.b: The murder of Sergei Kirov in December 1934 gave Stalin the pretext for a wave of arrests, and the first public trial took place in August 1936.
points: Sergei Kirov, the Leningrad party leader and a close associate of Stalin, was shot dead in Leningrad on 1 December 1934.
The NKVD blamed the murder on a conspiracy of former Zinovievists, and many oppositionists were arrested and shot without trial in the weeks that followed.
The first show trial, of Grigory Zinoviev, Lev Kamenev and others, took place in August 1936 in the Hall of Columns in Moscow.
The defendants confessed to plotting with Trotsky, to terrorism and to working with foreign powers, and sixteen were sentenced to death and executed.
The prosecutor Andrei Vyshinsky, later Soviet Foreign Minister, dominated the proceedings and demanded the death penalty in each case.
Trotsky, living in exile, was condemned in absentia, and the trial supplied material for Soviet propaganda against him and his supporters abroad.

notes.b: Two further trials in 1937 and 1938 extended the charges to economic managers and to the leaders of the Right Opposition.
points: The second trial, of Yuri Pyatakov, Karl Radek and others, was held in January 1937 and was used to accuse them of sabotage in industry and of links with Trotsky.
Pyatakov, a deputy commissar for heavy industry, was executed after the trial, and Radek received a ten-year sentence and died in a camp in 1939.
The military purge began in June 1937 with the trial and execution of Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky and other senior officers, accused of conspiring with Germany and Japan.
The third trial, of Nikolai Bukharin, Alexei Rykov, Genrikh Yagoda and others, took place in March 1938 and was the last major public trial.
Bukharin and Rykov were charged with plotting to assassinate Lenin and Stalin and with conspiring with foreign intelligence, and were executed.
Yagoda, who had led the NKVD until 1936, was tried and shot in March 1938 after being accused of treason.

notes.h: How confessions were obtained and how the trials were staged
notes.b: The trials were scripted and the defendants' confessions were extracted through torture, threats against families and promises of leniency.
points: Defendants were held in NKVD prisons for months, often deprived of sleep, and subjected to beatings and threats against their wives and children.
Confessions were drafted by the NKVD and rehearsed in advance, and defendants who resisted were told that their families would suffer.
The trials were held in public venues before selected audiences, with foreign journalists and diplomats present and Soviet newspapers reporting each stage.
Defendants who confessed were often promised that their lives would be spared, a promise that was not kept in the cases of the 1936 to 1938 trials.

Foreign observers, including some diplomats and journalists, reported the confessions as credible, while others such as the Dewey Commission in Mexico investigated the charges and concluded that they were false.
The American philosopher John Dewey led the commission of inquiry in Mexico in 1937, which heard Trotsky's defence and found the accusations unfounded.

notes.h: The wider Terror and the impact on the Soviet system
notes.b: The show trials were part of a Terror that reached into the party, the army, the economy and ordinary families, leaving lasting effects on Soviet life.
points: The Great Terror of 1937 and 1938 saw mass arrests and executions carried out under quotas set by Moscow, and the NKVD's Order 00447 of July 1937 set targets for arrests and executions in each region.
Hundreds of thousands of people were shot, and many more were sent to labour camps in the Gulag system, where conditions were harsh and mortality high.

About 1.5 million people were arrested in 1937 and 1938, and about 680,000 were executed in those two years, according to figures later released by the Soviet authorities; the figures are disputed and remain approximate.
The Central Committee and the Politburo lost many members, and a large share of the delegates to the 1934 Party Congress were arrested or shot by 1939.
The army lost a large part of its senior officer corps, including most of its marshals and many commanders of military districts, a weakness that the Germans later exploited in 1941.
Yezhov himself was removed in late 1938, tried and shot in 1940, and Lavrentiy Beria replaced him as head of the NKVD, ending the most intense phase of the Terror.

notes.b: The show trials established Stalin's absolute authority and created a climate of fear, but they also weakened the institutions the regime needed for war.
points: The trials removed Stalin's last serious rivals within the party and confirmed the personal dominance of his leadership.
The climate of fear discouraged criticism and made officials cautious, reducing the independent initiative that the economy and the army needed.
Foreign communists were deeply affected, as the trials divided communist parties abroad and led many to reject the Soviet line.

Contemporary opinion in the West was divided: many liberal and socialist observers condemned the trials as frame-ups, while some communist sympathisers and Western visitors accepted the official account.
Later historians have treated the trials as the clearest example of the totalitarian system, and archival research after 1989 showed that many confessions had been fabricated.
The show trials are a key case study for the personality cult and totalitarianism, since they show how Stalin used terror and propaganda together to control the party and society.

notes.h: Assessment: the Terror and Soviet strength
notes.b: Judgements of the show trials weigh the consolidation of Stalin's power and the discipline of the state against the damage done to the party, the army and the economy.
points: Achievement for Stalin: by 1939 his dominance over the party and state was complete, and the regime had no organised opposition inside the Soviet Union.
Limit for the regime: the purge of the army and the loss of experienced managers and officials weakened the Soviet Union in its first years of war with Germany.
Contemporary view: many Western communists defended the trials as necessary to root out traitors, while liberal critics called them an open travesty of justice.

Later view: historians after 1989 have treated the trials as a deliberate campaign of terror, though they continue to debate how far Stalin planned it in advance and how far local officials acted on their own.

keyTerms.definition: A public trial in which the verdict is decided in advance and defendants are made to confess, so that the trial serves as propaganda.
The removal of members from a party, state or army, often by arrest and execution, to eliminate rivals or suspected opponents.
A system in which the state seeks to control every aspect of public and private life through a single party, secret police and propaganda.
The organised spread of information and images to shape opinion and promote a regime, its leader and its policies.
The promotion of a leader as an infallible and heroic figure, shown through propaganda, rituals and his image in public life.
The Soviet people's commissariat for internal affairs, which combined the secret police with the labour camp system and carried out the arrests and executions of the Terror.
The Soviet system of labour camps, administered by the NKVD, in which millions of prisoners were held and forced to work.
